messages.author: b7d8701fe15f0b01
messages.subject: Variable selection for hierarchical model
parts:
Hi,

I understand I can use backward elimination process to remove insignificant variables from my model based on values like the DIC.
However, when I have a mixed effect model, how should I go about variable selection?

I am unsure whether I should:

1. Use a simple fixed effect model for variable selection first, then construct a mixed effect model from this fixed effect model?
2. Or should I use the mixed effect model find the best set of mixed effect variables, then eliminate some insignificant fixed effect variables?

Many thanks

messages.author: fd5b3eee58ac5e83
messages.subject: Re: Variable selection for hierarchical model
parts:
Hi,
I am not an expert at all, but I would always do the second approach that you are describing. The reason is that if you do not include any mixed effects in the models that you use to decide which fixed effects are important (your version 1), it seems that you are using a model that might not fit your data well in general to do this variable selection. 

I would do two steps, first find the best model without any fixed effects, and then select the fixed effects based on the basemodel that was selected. 

I have done this in a few previous studies and also find it more easy to follow compared to finding the best model across fixed and random effects at the same time. 

Happy to learn and hear from others if this is not a good approach.
Brigitte

messages.author: 5063972801d34964
messages.subject: RE: [r-inla] Re: Variable selection for hierarchical model
parts:
Inclusion or exclusion of a covariate, fixed or random, should always be based on what question you truly want to ask (the model often is answering a different one than you think!) rather than just getting better information criteria scores.

 

With that said, if you feel good about your candidate predictors and truly want just to find the most effective combination, with INLA the best option I suspect is WAIC.  Run the model with and without various fixed and random effects, tracking the change in WAIC for each one.  If the variable is useless, the WAIC will go up by ~2 points.  If it is of dubious usefulness, WAIC will go up  by less than 2 points or move downward only trivially, if at all.  If adding a variable makes the WAIC go down by at least a few points, it is probably an improvement.  WAIC is preferred because it more effectively considers the “partial” parameter effect that random effects have rather than using the “each parameter counts for 1” assumption that undergirds most fixed effects criteria like AIC and I think DIC also. I would not use those except for the quick and dirty analyses, like with lme4.  They often still work surprisingly well even on multilevel models, but they can be fooled sometimes.

 

So:

 

  1. Use WAIC when employing INLA as a first-line model comparator;
  2. Start with what you think is your single best predictor, fixed or random, fit a model to it, and then add more predictors in declining order of expected helpfulness in successive models: what happens to the WAIC each time you do that?  If it helps, leave it in, if it doesn’t, take it out.
  3. When you are done considering all the candidate variables in this sequence, consider retrying some of the ones you discarded which you had thought would be helpful.  In other words, if you end up using three predictors, but one of the other variables surprised you with its unhelpfulness the first round, try adding it back in one more time to the three you did choose. It’s possible that some of the others you later added helped unmask the effect of this variable. If it still doesn’t matter, then you have your answer.
  4. Ideally you would do a grid search that explores literally all possible combinations but sometimes that is not practical. 

 

In general, simpler models are better (that’s the whole premise of penalized information criteria) so I suggest including only those predictors in the final model that substantially move the needle (e.g., drop the WAIC by a fair amount). This also makes models faster to run.

 

Plenty of exceptions to what I just said, but one of the main advantages of INLA is its speediness which makes it useful for model comparison. This is one way to use it effectively.

 

Jonathan
